name: Photon Absorption
description: A photon is absorbed by a hydrogen atom, exciting the electron from 1s to 2p

layman.title: Catching Light
layman.summary: Watch a particle of light get swallowed by a hydrogen atom

sections.whatsHappening: A photon — a tiny packet of light energy — is flying toward a hydrogen atom. When it arrives, the atom absorbs it completely. The photon vanishes, and its energy is transferred to the electron, which jumps to a higher energy level. Watch the electron cloud change shape from a sphere (1s) to a dumbbell (2p).
sections.whyItMatters: This is the basic process behind how atoms and molecules absorb light. It's why leaves are green (their chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light), and the dark lines it leaves in starlight tell astronomers which elements a star contains. Many colors you see exist because atoms and molecules absorb specific wavelengths of light. (Solids such as solar cells absorb a whole range of energies instead of one exact value, because their electrons share bands of levels.)
sections.whatToWatch: Follow the yellow photon as it approaches from the left. Notice its wave-like trail — light behaves as both a wave and a particle. When it reaches the atom, it disappears and the blue electron cloud quickly changes from a round sphere to an elongated dumbbell shape.
sections.funFact: The atom can only absorb a photon with exactly the right energy to lift the electron to another orbital: 10.2 electron volts in this case. A little too much or too little, and the photon passes right through, like a vending machine that only accepts exact change. A photon with more than 13.6 eV is different: it can knock the electron out of the atom altogether.

scientific.narrative: A photon with energy E=10.2 eV (corresponding to the Lyman-alpha transition) is incident on a hydrogen atom in the ground state (n=1, l=0, m=0). The photon energy exactly matches the energy difference between the n=1 and n=2 levels: ΔE = 13.6(1/1² - 1/2²) = 10.2 eV. Upon absorption, the electron transitions to the 2p state (n=2, l=1, m=0), which has a characteristic dumbbell-shaped probability distribution aligned along the y-axis. The 2p cloud's 90% surface is drawn at 7.99 a₀ (423 pm).

simplifications: The photon is absorbed when it reaches the nucleus. Real absorption has no single point of impact.
